1. Social Problems — Meaning

  • A social problem is a condition that adversely affects a significant section of society and requires collective action for its solution.
  • Social problems arise from interactions among economic, social, cultural, institutional and political factors.
  • They should not be viewed merely as individual difficulties.
📌 Must-Memorise

Social Problem → Wider Social Impact + Collective Response

2. Personal Difficulty vs Social Problem

  • A personal difficulty may affect an individual or household without reflecting a wider structural pattern.
  • A problem becomes social when it affects large sections of society or is produced by wider institutions and social structures.
  • Unemployment affecting one person can be personal; widespread unemployment becomes a major social and economic problem.

3. Major Social Problems

Important examples include:

  • Caste discrimination.
  • Gender inequality.
  • Child labour.
  • Child marriage.
  • Bonded labour.
  • Human trafficking.
  • Substance abuse.
  • Homelessness.
  • Disability-related exclusion.
  • Vulnerability of senior citizens.

4. Social Problems — Interconnected Nature

Social problems often reinforce one another.

For example:

Poverty

→ Child Labour

→ Reduced Education

→ Low-Skill Employment

→ Continued Poverty

📌 Must-Memorise

Social Problems → Often Interlinked, Not Isolated

5. Economic Growth and Social Inclusion

  • Economic development is not measured only by growth in income.
  • It must also improve opportunities, dignity, quality of life and access to basic services.
  • Unequal growth can leave large groups excluded from development.
📌 Must-Memorise

Economic Growth + Social Inclusion → Sustainable Development

6. Social Problems — Economic Consequences

Social problems can:

  • Reduce labour productivity.
  • Limit education.
  • Lower labour-force participation.
  • Increase household expenditure on illness or addiction.
  • Weaken community cooperation.
  • Discourage investment during social conflict.

7. Social Inequality — Meaning

  • Social inequality means unequal access to resources, opportunities, status and power.

It can arise on the basis of:

  • Caste.
  • Gender.
  • Income.
  • Region.
  • Disability.
  • Education.
  • Occupation.
  • Social background.

8. Social Exclusion — Meaning

  • Social exclusion occurs when individuals or groups are prevented from participating fully in economic, social or political life.

Exclusion can affect access to:

  • Education.
  • Employment.
  • Housing.
  • Credit.
  • Health care.
  • Public spaces.
  • Political participation.

9. Intergenerational Disadvantage

  • Social exclusion can persist across generations.
  • Children from disadvantaged households may inherit poorer access to nutrition, health, education and employment.
📌 Must-Memorise

Exclusion → Reduced Opportunity → Persistent Disadvantage

10. Constitutional Equality Framework

Important constitutional provisions include:

  • Article 14 → Equality before law and equal protection of laws.
  • Article 15 → Prohibition of discrimination on specified grounds.
  • Article 16 → Equality of opportunity in public employment.
  • Article 17 → Abolition of untouchability.
📌 Must-Memorise

14 → Equality

15 → Non-Discrimination

16 → Public Employment

17 → Untouchability

11. Article 17 — Abolition of Untouchability

  • Article 17 abolishes untouchability.
  • Its practice in any form is constitutionally forbidden.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 17 → Abolition of Untouchability

12. Protection of Civil Rights Act — 1955

  • The Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955 provides legal measures against practices arising from untouchability.
📌 Must-Memorise

Protection of Civil Rights Act → 1955

13. SC/ST Prevention of Atrocities Act — 1989

  • The Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989 provides stronger protection against specified offences and atrocities against members of SCs and STs.
📌 Must-Memorise

SC/ST Prevention of Atrocities Act → 1989

14. Civil Rights Act vs Atrocities Act

  • Protection of Civil Rights Act → 1955 → Practices arising from untouchability.
  • SC/ST Prevention of Atrocities Act → 1989 → Specified atrocities against SCs and STs.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

1955 Act ≠ 1989 Act

15. Caste Discrimination — Wider Response

Reducing caste discrimination requires:

  • Law.
  • Enforcement.
  • Education.
  • Social reform.
  • Economic empowerment.
  • Political participation.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Law Alone ≠ Complete Social Reform

16. Gender Inequality — Meaning

Gender inequality can appear in:

  • Education.
  • Employment.
  • Wages.
  • Property ownership.
  • Nutrition.
  • Health care.
  • Household decision-making.
  • Political participation.

17. Constitutional Protection for Women

Important provisions include:

  • Article 14 → Equality.
  • Article 15 → Prohibition of discrimination including on grounds of sex.
  • Article 15(3) → Permits special provisions for women and children.
  • Article 16 → Equal opportunity in public employment.
  • Article 39 → Directive Principles relating to livelihood and equal-pay principles.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 15(3) → Special Provisions for Women and Children

18. Gender Equality — Economic Importance

  • Women's access to education, employment, property, credit and entrepreneurship can raise household income and overall productivity.
  • Gender equality is both a social-justice and economic-development objective.

19. Violence Against Women — Major Forms

Violence can include:

  • Domestic violence.
  • Sexual harassment.
  • Sexual assault.
  • Dowry-related violence.
  • Trafficking.
  • Stalking.
  • Cyber harassment.

20. Dowry Prohibition Act — 1961

  • The Dowry Prohibition Act was enacted in 1961.
  • It addresses dowry-related practices.
📌 Must-Memorise

Dowry Prohibition Act → 1961

21. Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act — 2005

  • The Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act was enacted in 2005.
  • It provides legal remedies and protection against domestic violence.
📌 Must-Memorise

Domestic Violence Act → 2005

22. Workplace Sexual Harassment Act — 2013

  • The Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act was enacted in 2013.
  • It creates a framework to prevent and address workplace sexual harassment.
📌 Must-Memorise

Workplace Sexual Harassment Act → 2013

23. Women's Protection Law Memory Chain

  • 1961 → Dowry Prohibition.
  • 2005 → Domestic Violence.
  • 2013 → Workplace Sexual Harassment.
📌 Must-Memorise

1961 → 2005 → 2013

24. Child Labour — Meaning and Causes

  • Child labour refers to work by children in circumstances prohibited by law or harmful to education, health or development.

Major causes can include:

  • Poverty.
  • Household debt.
  • Migration.
  • Lack of educational access.
  • Informal employment.
  • Demand for cheap labour.

25. Article 24 — Child Labour Protection

  • Article 24 prohibits employment of children below fourteen years in factories, mines and other constitutionally specified hazardous employment.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 24 → Protection Against Child Employment in Specified Settings

26. Article 21A — Education

  • Article 21A provides free and compulsory education for children between 6 and 14 years.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 21A → Education → Age 6–14

27. Child Labour — Poverty Cycle

Low Household Income

→ Child Labour

→ Reduced Education

→ Low-Skill Employment

→ Continued Poverty

Breaking the cycle requires:

  • Education.
  • Income security.
  • Enforcement.
  • Social support.

28. Child Marriage — Meaning and Consequences

Child marriage can reduce:

  • Educational continuation.
  • Health outcomes.
  • Economic independence.
  • Employment opportunities.
  • Long-term human development.

29. Prohibition of Child Marriage Act — 2006

  • The Prohibition of Child Marriage Act was enacted in 2006.
📌 Must-Memorise

Prohibition of Child Marriage Act → 2006

30. Child Marriage — Prevention Strategy

Prevention requires:

  • Law enforcement.
  • Education.
  • Public awareness.
  • Women's empowerment.
  • Household economic security.
  • Community participation.

31. Article 23 — Trafficking and Forced Labour

  • Article 23 prohibits:
  • Traffic in human beings.
  • Begar.
  • Other similar forms of forced labour.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 23 → Trafficking + Begar + Forced Labour

32. Bonded Labour — Meaning

  • Bonded labour occurs when a person is compelled to work because of debt or another coercive obligation.
  • The person may not be free to leave until the debt is considered repaid.

33. Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act — 1976

  • The Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act was enacted in 1976.
  • It abolished the bonded-labour system and provided for extinguishment of bonded debt according to law.
📌 Must-Memorise

Bonded Labour Act → 1976

34. Bonded Labour — Causes of Persistence

Bonded labour can persist because of:

  • Poverty.
  • Debt.
  • Social inequality.
  • Informal labour arrangements.
  • Weak enforcement.

35. Human Trafficking — Meaning

  • Human trafficking involves recruitment, transportation, transfer, harbouring or receipt of persons through prohibited means for exploitation.

It can involve:

  • Sexual exploitation.
  • Forced labour.
  • Domestic servitude.
  • Child exploitation.
  • Other coercive exploitation.

36. Trafficking vs Voluntary Migration

  • Trafficking → Coercion, deception or exploitation.
  • Voluntary migration → Movement for work, education, marriage, safety or other reasons without trafficking exploitation.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Human Trafficking ≠ Voluntary Migration

37. Trafficking — Vulnerability Factors

Risk can increase because of:

  • Poverty.
  • Unemployment.
  • Family distress.
  • Migration.
  • Social exclusion.
  • Lack of awareness.
  • Organised criminal networks.

38. Substance Abuse — Meaning and Effects

  • Substance abuse refers to harmful or dependent use of alcohol, narcotic drugs or other intoxicating substances.

It can affect:

  • Physical health.
  • Mental well-being.
  • Employment.
  • Household income.
  • Family relationships.
  • Public safety.

39. Article 47 — Public Health and Intoxicants

  • Article 47 directs the State to endeavour to improve public health and work towards prohibition of intoxicating drinks and drugs injurious to health, except for medicinal purposes.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 47 → Public Health + Intoxicants

40. Substance-Abuse Response

Effective policy requires:

Prevention

  • Regulation
  • Treatment
  • Rehabilitation
  • Awareness
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Substance Abuse ≠ Law-Enforcement Issue Alone

41. Senior Citizens — Major Social Challenges

Senior citizens can face:

  • Income insecurity.
  • Health needs.
  • Social isolation.
  • Neglect.
  • Abuse.
  • Reduced mobility.
  • Dependence on others.

42. Senior Citizens Act — 2007

  • The Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act was enacted in 2007.
  • It provides a legal framework relating to maintenance and welfare of parents and senior citizens.
📌 Must-Memorise

Senior Citizens Act → 2007

43. Ageing — Wider Welfare Requirement

Ageing policy also needs:

  • Health care.
  • Pensions.
  • Accessible housing.
  • Mobility.
  • Social care.
  • Dignity.
  • Social participation.

44. Disability — Rights-Based Approach

  • Persons with disabilities can face barriers in education, employment, transport, buildings, communication and public services.
  • The modern approach focuses on rights and inclusion rather than charity alone.

45. Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act — 2016

  • The Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act was enacted in 2016.
  • It strengthened the rights-based framework for equality, accessibility and participation.
📌 Must-Memorise

Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act → 2016

46. Disability Inclusion — Core Principles

The rights-based approach emphasises:

  • Equality.
  • Dignity.
  • Accessibility.
  • Education.
  • Employment.
  • Participation.
  • Reasonable accommodation.

47. Accessibility — Meaning

Accessibility can include:

  • Ramps.
  • Accessible transport.
  • Sign-language support.
  • Screen-reader-compatible digital services.
  • Accessible toilets.
  • Appropriate educational support.

48. Migration — Meaning and Types

Migration can be:

  • Rural to urban.
  • Rural to rural.
  • Urban to urban.
  • Urban to rural.
  • Inter-State.
  • Intra-State.

People may migrate for:

  • Employment.
  • Education.
  • Marriage.
  • Safety.
  • Better opportunities.

49. Migration — Benefits and Vulnerabilities

Migration can:

  • Improve employment opportunities.
  • Move labour from low-productivity to higher-productivity activities.

But migrants can also face:

  • Insecure work.
  • Poor housing.
  • Weak social protection.
  • Language barriers.
  • Difficulty accessing services.

50. Urbanisation — Not Automatically a Social Problem

  • Urbanisation can create employment and economic opportunities.
  • The social problem arises when urban growth exceeds planning, housing and infrastructure capacity.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Urbanisation ≠ Automatically Harmful

51. Unplanned Urbanisation — Problems

Rapid unplanned urban growth can create:

  • Housing shortages.
  • Congestion.
  • Poor sanitation.
  • Drainage problems.
  • Waste-management problems.
  • Pressure on public services.

52. Slum Conditions

Slum households may experience inadequate:

  • Drinking water.
  • Sanitation.
  • Drainage.
  • Waste disposal.
  • Housing quality.
  • Health services.

53. Homelessness — Causes and Vulnerability

Homelessness may result from:

  • Extreme poverty.
  • Migration.
  • Family breakdown.
  • Disability.
  • Displacement.
  • Natural disasters.
  • Loss of livelihood.

Homeless persons face greater risks of:

  • Disease.
  • Violence.
  • Exploitation.
  • Exclusion from welfare services.

54. Begging and Social Vulnerability

  • Begging may be connected with poverty, homelessness, disability, abandonment, trafficking or lack of social support.
  • Long-term responses therefore require rehabilitation and social protection rather than only punitive action.

55. Social Vulnerability — Meaning

  • Social vulnerability means greater exposure to economic or social shocks because of inadequate resources or support systems.

Vulnerable groups can include:

  • Homeless persons.
  • Destitute elderly persons.
  • Orphaned children.
  • Persons with severe disabilities.
  • Trafficking survivors.
  • Abandoned persons.

56. Tamil Nadu — Social Reform Context

  • Tamil Nadu has a long history of social-reform movements challenging caste hierarchy, untouchability and unequal social status.
  • Self-Respect and Dravidian reform traditions influenced debates on equality, representation and dignity.
  • Detailed movement history belongs to the later dedicated chapter.

57. Tamil Nadu — Caste and Gender Concerns

Continuing concerns can include:

  • Caste discrimination.
  • Caste conflict.
  • Violence against women.
  • Unequal employment opportunities.
  • Unpaid care work.
  • Property inequality.
  • Safety concerns.

58. Tamil Nadu — Child and Alcohol-Related Concerns

Important social concerns include:

  • Child labour.
  • Child marriage.
  • School dropout.
  • Abuse.
  • Alcohol-related health and family problems.
  • Alcohol abuse can affect household finances, health, family relationships and public safety.

59. Tamil Nadu — Urban Social Challenges

Tamil Nadu's relatively high urbanisation creates challenges involving:

  • Affordable housing.
  • Congestion.
  • Waste management.
  • Migrant-worker accommodation.
  • Urban poverty.
  • Pressure on infrastructure.

60. Tamil Nadu — Elderly Welfare

  • Increasing life expectancy and demographic change make elderly welfare increasingly important.
  • Health care, pensions, social care and accessible infrastructure will become more significant.

61. Institutional Response to Social Problems

A durable response requires participation by:

  • Government.
  • Judiciary.
  • Local governments.
  • Civil society.
  • Schools.
  • Families.
  • Communities.
  • Media.

62. Role of Government and Judiciary

Government provides:

  • Laws.
  • Welfare schemes.
  • Enforcement.
  • Public services.
  • Social protection.

The judiciary:

  • Protects constitutional rights.
  • Interprets laws.
  • Provides legal remedies.

63. Role of Civil Society and Local Communities

Civil-society organisations can support:

  • Awareness.
  • Rehabilitation.
  • Legal assistance.
  • Community mobilisation.
  • Monitoring.
  • Support services.

Local communities can help challenge discrimination and exploitative practices.

64. Law, Enforcement and Social Change

  • Law establishes rights and minimum standards.
  • Laws become less effective when victims cannot access police, courts, legal aid or support institutions.
📌 Must-Memorise

Law + Enforcement + Awareness + Economic Opportunity + Social Change

65. Prevention — Long-Term Strategy

Social problems can be reduced through:

  • Education.
  • Employment.
  • Household income security.
  • Women's empowerment.
  • Social protection.
  • Effective law enforcement.
  • Community participation.

66. Inclusive Development — Core Idea

  • Inclusive development expands opportunities for disadvantaged groups rather than merely increasing total income.
  • The long-term goal is to remove conditions that produce exclusion.
📌 Must-Memorise

Economic Growth

  • Equal Opportunity
  • Social Protection
  • Dignity

= Inclusive Development

67. Constitutional Memory Chain

  • Article 14 → Equality.
  • Article 15 → Non-discrimination.
  • Article 15(3) → Special provisions for women and children.
  • Article 16 → Equality in public employment.
  • Article 17 → Untouchability abolished.
  • Article 21A → Education, age 6–14.
  • Article 23 → Trafficking + forced labour.
  • Article 24 → Child employment protection.
  • Article 47 → Public health + intoxicants.

68. Social-Law Timeline Memory Chain

  • 1955 → Protection of Civil Rights Act.
  • 1961 → Dowry Prohibition Act.
  • 1976 → Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act.
  • 1989 → SC/ST Prevention of Atrocities Act.
  • 2005 → Domestic Violence Act.
  • 2006 → Prohibition of Child Marriage Act.
  • 2007 → Senior Citizens Act.
  • 2013 → Workplace Sexual Harassment Act.
  • 2016 → Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act.

69. TNPSC Traps

  • A social problem is broader than a private personal difficulty.
  • Social problems can be interconnected.
  • Economic growth does not automatically remove social exclusion.
  • Article 14 → Equality.
  • Article 15 → Non-discrimination.
  • Article 16 → Equality of opportunity in public employment.
  • Article 17 → Abolition of untouchability.
  • Protection of Civil Rights Act → 1955.
  • SC/ST Prevention of Atrocities Act → 1989.
  • Article 15(3) allows special provisions for women and children.
  • Dowry Prohibition Act → 1961.
  • Domestic Violence Act → 2005.
  • Workplace Sexual Harassment Act → 2013.
  • Article 21A → Free and compulsory education for ages 6–14.
  • Article 24 concerns constitutionally prohibited child employment.
  • Child labour and child marriage are different social problems.
  • Prohibition of Child Marriage Act → 2006.
  • Article 23 → Trafficking, begar and forced labour.
  • Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act → 1976.
  • Trafficking is not the same as voluntary migration.
  • Article 47 is a Directive Principle concerning public health and intoxicants.
  • Substance dependence needs treatment and rehabilitation in addition to enforcement.
  • Senior Citizens Act → 2007.
  • Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act → 2016.
  • Disability should be approached through rights and accessibility, not merely charity.
  • Urbanisation is not automatically a social problem.
  • Unplanned urbanisation creates housing and infrastructure pressures.
  • Homelessness cannot be understood only as lack of income.
  • Social legislation needs enforcement and institutional access.
  • Tamil Nadu's social-reform history is relevant to caste equality, gender equality and dignity.
  • Social problems require legal, economic, educational and social responses together.

  • 24 → Child Employment Protection.
  • Child Marriage Act → 2006.
  • 23 → Trafficking + Forced Labour.
  • Bonded Labour Act → 1976.
  • 47 → Public Health + Intoxicants.
  • Senior Citizens Act → 2007.
  • Disability Rights Act → 2016.
  • Urbanisation ≠ Unplanned Urbanisation.
